title: CHAPTER 2 : IS MATTER AROUND US PURE?

blocks.content: 1. INTRODUCTION

In our daily life, we use many substances such as water, milk, air, salt, sugar, soil and food items.

Although these substances appear simple, they are not always pure in the scientific sense.



In chemistry, the word “pure” does not mean clean or hygienic.

A pure substance is one which contains only one kind of particles and has a fixed composition and fixed properties.
2. PURE SUBSTANCE

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Pure substances consist of only one type of constituent particle and are classified as elements or compounds.
Homogeneous mixtures possess a uniform composition throughout, whereas colloids are heterogeneous systems.
The Tyndall Effect refers to the scattering of light by suspended colloidal particles.
Compounds are formed by the chemical combination of two or more elements in a fixed ratio by mass.
Physical changes alter physical properties without forming new substances, while chemical changes produce entirely new chemical entities.

blocks.content:
A pure substance is a substance that is made up of only one type of particles.

It has a fixed chemical composition and definite physical and chemical properties.

Pure substances cannot be separated into simpler substances by physical methods.

Examples of pure substances include:

• Distilled water

• Oxygen gas

• Gold

• Sodium chloride
3. TYPES OF PURE SUBSTANCES

Pure substances are broadly classified into two types:

1. Elements

2. Compounds
3.1 ELEMENT

An element is a pure substance that is made up of only one type of atom.

Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances by any chemical method.



Examples of elements include hydrogen, oxygen, iron, copper and gold.

Elements are further classified into three types:

• Metals

• Non-metals

• Metalloids
3.2 COMPOUND

A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio.

The properties of a compound are completely different from the properties of the elements that form it.

For example, hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water, which has entirely different properties from both hydrogen and oxygen.

4. MIXTURE

A mixture is a substance formed by mixing two or more substances in any proportion.

In a mixture, the components do not combine chemically.

The components of a mixture retain their individual properties and can be separated by physical methods.

5. TYPES OF MIXTURE
IS MATTER AROUND US PURE?

Mixtures are classified into two main types:

1. Homogeneous mixture

2. Heterogeneous mixture
5.1 HOMOGENEOUS MIXTURE

A homogeneous mixture is a mixture in which the composition is uniform throughout.

The components cannot be distinguished with naked eyes.

Examples of homogeneous mixtures include salt solution, sugar solution and air.
5.2 HETEROGENEOUS MIXTURE

A heterogeneous mixture is a mixture in which the composition is not uniform.

The different components can be easily seen.

Examples include sand and water, oil and water, and soil.
6. SOLUTION

rows: One or more new substances are formed

blocks.content:
A solution is a homogeneous mixture formed by dissolving one substance in another.

A solution has two components:

• Solute – the substance that gets dissolved

• Solvent – the substance in which the solute dissolves

For example, in salt solution, salt is the solute and water is the solvent.
7. SUSPENSION

A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture in which solid particles are dispersed in a liquid.

The particles of a suspension are large and can be seen with naked eyes.

These particles settle down when the mixture is left undisturbed.

Example: Muddy water
8. COLLOID

A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture in which the particles are very small and cannot be seen with naked eyes.

The particles of a colloid do not settle down on standing.

Examples of colloids include milk, fog, smoke and blood.
9. TYNDALL EFFECT

The scattering of light by colloidal particles is known as the Tyndall effect.

This effect helps to distinguish between a true solution and a colloidal solution.

True solutions do not show Tyndall effect, while colloids do.
10. METHODS OF SEPARATION OF MIXTURES

Different components of a mixture can be separated using various physical methods.

Some common methods of separation include:

• Filtration

• Evaporation

• Distillation

• Centrifugation

• Chromatography

• Sublimation

blocks.content: 11. PHYSICAL AND CHEMICAL CHANGES

A physical change is a change in which no new substance is formed.

The change is usually temporary and reversible.

A chemical change is a change in which a new substance is formed.

The change is permanent and irreversible.
12. IMPORTANT  EXAM POINTS

• Pure substances have fixed composition.

• Mixtures can be separated by physical methods.

• Colloids show Tyndall effect.

• Distillation is used to separate liquids.

• Chromatography is used to separate coloured substances.
13. QUICK REVISION

• A pure substance contains only one kind of particles.

• Elements and compounds are pure substances.

• Mixtures are of two types – homogeneous and heterogeneous.

• Colloids show Tyndall effect.

• Separation methods depend on the nature of mixture.
